subject: RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables
parts:
Currently, when using rstan, you can either package the data variables in a list that is then supplied as the value of the "data" argument to rstan::sampling(), OR you can define your data variables in the global environment and rely on rstan::sampling() to find them there. While the latter behaviour makes for fewer keystrokes, I encountered a scenario while teaching today that I believe strongly argues against it. 

I had students run the same model twice, once with the data in its raw format, once after rescaling the data (using scale() in R) . The .stan file expected a data variable called Y for the outcome data, and the first time students packaged the data, in its raw format, they indeed named an element in the list "Y". But the second time around, having created a rescaled version of Y they called Y_rescaled, and erroneously created a list that had an element named "Y_rescaled" instead of the expected "Y". However, since an object called Y still existed in the global environment, when stan::sampling couldn't find an entry in the list called "Y", it went and found the object called "Y" still in the global environment, yielding no warning or error and subsequent samples for which the priors were dramatically ill posed (since the priors were specified expecting scaled data).

The only reason we caught this error is because some students didn't make the error and some did, yielding different results for different students despite everyone using the same seed. Had they been home working alone, I think it unlikely that they would have caught it.

Admittedly, you can never prevent all user errors, but since seeking variables in the global environment is a convenience feature that frankly defies expected behaviour from well-contained programming systems, I wonder if it might be considered for removal.

Cheers,

Mike


--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables
parts:
Hi, this could be best to discuss face to face, but very briefly:

What I would like is for the stan() call in R to take variables from the local environment. Thus, if you're operating in the R console entering commands one at a time, it would use the global environment; if you're calling stan() from within a function, it will take variables from the local environment; etc. It should also be possible to input the data as a list.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables
parts:
On Wednesday, October 19, 2016 at 4:32:05 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
What I would like is for the stan() call in R to take variables from the local environment.  Thus, if you're operating in the R console entering commands one at a time, it would use the global environment; if you're calling stan() from within a function, it will take variables from the local environment; etc.  It should also be possible to input the data as a list.

It already does all that. The problem is that the global environment is an ancestor of all environments (except package namespaces). So, even if you first look in the local environment, that only works if the thing is in the local environment. Otherwise, it will continue looking in the next environment up until it finds a R object with the same name. Also, it wouldn't make any difference in the OP's case because stan() was being typed in the global environment.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan suggestion: don't look in global environment for data variables
parts:
Andrew's right. It reads the global environment.

If I run this R code in RStan 2.12.1:

stan_program <- "data { real mu; } parameters { real y; } model { y ~ normal(mu, 1); }";
mu <- 5;
run_program <- function (x) { mu <- -5; stan(model_code=stan_program); }
mu <- 0;
fit <- run_program();
print(fit);

I see this:

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y 0.00 0.02 1.03 -1.95 -0.72 0.00 0.68 1.99 3225 1

So the no-arg version is just reading mu out of the global environment, not out of
the function's.

On the other hand, if I do this:

run_program <- function (x) { mu <- -5; stan(model_code=stan_program, data=c("mu")); }

then I get

mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat
y -5.01 0.02 1.02 -6.99 -5.69 -4.99 -4.33 -2.99 2958 1

So the one that reads by name uses the local environment.

I'd prefer the local environment behavior in both places.

- Bob
